1279: When fasting, the operation is reversed: a phosphate detaches the terminal glucose. The liver will release it into the blood.
1280: Phosphorolysis, by a pyridoxal phosphate enzyme activated by phosphorylation under glucagon (PKA, then phosphorylase kinase). Glucose-1-phosphate becomes glucose-6-phosphate again, then glucose thanks to the glucose-6-phosphatase of the reticulum. Deficiencies: Hers and von Gierke diseases.
1281: Why does muscle not release glucose into the blood?
1286: In the neuronal membrane, this pump maintains the sodium and potassium gradients on which the action potential depends.
1287: Each cycle: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP used. In the neuron it uses a large share of the ATP.
1289: The pump loads three sodium ions on the cytosolic side, phosphorylates itself using one ATP, flips, and releases them outside.
1290: P-type ATPase: the γ phosphate of ATP is transferred to an aspartate of the α subunit, which switches the pump from the E1 state, open to the cytosol with high affinity for Na⁺, to the E2-P state, open to the outside.
1291: On which residue does the pump phosphorylate itself?
1294: Two potassium ions take their place; the phosphate comes off, the pump flips back and releases them into the cytosol.
1295: K⁺ binding triggers dephosphorylation. An electrogenic pump (3 Na⁺ for 2 K⁺), locked in the E2-P state by ouabain and digoxin.
1301: Peroxisomal oxidases produce hydrogen peroxide; catalase destroys it on the spot.
1302: Catalase destroys hydrogen peroxide, a dangerous oxidant: two molecules give water and oxygen.
1303: A haem tetramer, one of the fastest enzymes known (millions of molecules per second). The first H₂O₂ oxidises the iron to compound I (Fe⁴⁺=O and a porphyrin radical); the second reduces it and releases O₂.
1304: Which metal sits at the active site?
1308: The chemical move that RNA polymerase II repeats at each nucleotide, about thirty times per second.
1309: RNA(n) + NTP → RNA(n + 1) + 2 Pi: two high-energy bonds spent per nucleotide added.
1311: The end of the RNA attacks a new nucleotide: a bond forms and two phosphates are released together.
1312: The 3′-OH, activated by a first Mg²⁺, attacks the α phosphate of the NTP paired with the template strand; a second Mg²⁺ stabilises the leaving pyrophosphate (the two-metal-ion mechanism shared by polymerases). The trigger loop closes over the correct NTP: one basis of fidelity.
1316: The pyrophosphate is cut at once into two phosphates: the reaction can no longer go backwards.
1317: Pyrophosphate hydrolysis (ΔG°′ ≈ −19 kJ/mol) makes polymerisation irreversible. When stalled, the polymerase can backtrack, and TFIIS makes it cleave the end of the RNA to restart.
1323: Three reactions, as soon as the RNA emerges from the polymerase, protect its 5′ end and prepare it for translation.
1324: m⁷GpppN: a methylated guanosine, linked head to head through three phosphates.
1326: The first nucleotide of the RNA carries three phosphates. The capping enzyme removes one.
1327: 5′-triphosphatase activity of RNGTT, recruited by the Ser5-phosphorylated CTD of the polymerase as soon as the RNA reaches 20 to 25 nucleotides.
1328: Which CTD mark recruits the capping enzyme?
1330: A guanosine is attached backwards, head to head, onto the end of the RNA: a 5′–5′ linkage.
1331: The enzyme first forms a covalent lysine–GMP adduct, then transfers it onto the 5′-diphosphate: a 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge, resistant to 5′→3′ exonucleases.
1332: Through which intermediate does the GMP pass?
1335: Finally, a methyl group is added to the guanine: the m⁷G cap is complete.
1336: RNMT (with RAM) methylates nitrogen 7 using S-adenosylmethionine. The positive charge created is recognised by the CBC complex in the nucleus, then by eIF4E in the cytoplasm. CMTR1 then methylates the 2′-OH of the first nucleotide.
1337: Which cytoplasmic factor recognises the cap?
1339: Five reactions that write or erase marks on DNA and histones, without touching the sequence.
1340: Methyl on DNA or H3K27: gene rather silent. Acetyl on histones: gene accessible. All these marks are reversible.
1342: A methyl group is added to a cytosine of DNA. In a promoter, this mark helps switch the gene off.
1343: The cytosine of a CpG dinucleotide is flipped out of the helix; a cysteine of the enzyme attacks carbon 6, which activates carbon 5 to receive the methyl from SAM. DNMT1, guided by UHRF1, copies the mark after replication; DNMT3A and 3B establish it.
1344: Which carbon of cytosine is methylated?
1349: The mark can be removed in steps: a TET enzyme first oxidises the methyl to hydroxymethyl.
1350: TET1–3, using Fe²⁺ and α-ketoglutarate: 5mC → 5hmC → 5fC → 5caC, bases excised by the glycosylase TDG then replaced by a cytosine. The 2-hydroxyglutarate from mutant IDH, succinate and fumarate inhibit them; vitamin C stimulates them.
1351: Which co-substrate do TET enzymes use?
1355: On histones, an acetyl group neutralises the charge of a lysine: chromatin loosens and the gene becomes accessible.
1356: p300/CBP acetylate in particular H3K27 at active enhancers and promoters. Acetyl-lysine is read by bromodomains (BRD4). Since the donor is acetyl-CoA, acetylation reflects the metabolic state of the cell.
1362: The mark is reversible: a deacetylase removes the acetyl, and chromatin closes again.
1363: Class I, II and IV HDACs are zinc hydrolases, inhibited by vorinostat and valproic acid. Sirtuins (class III) use NAD⁺ and release nicotinamide.
1366: A lysine can also receive one, two or three methyls. Depending on the lysine, the message is “active” or “silent”.
1367: H3K4me3 (SET1/MLL) marks active promoters, H3K36me3 (SETD2) the body of transcribed genes, H3K27me3 (EZH2, PRC2 complex) and H3K9me3 repressed chromatin. Methylation does not change the charge: it is read by chromodomains and PHD domains. Demethylases use FAD (LSD1) or Fe²⁺ and α-ketoglutarate (JmjC).
1370: Five reactions of the nucleolus: polymerase I extends the pre-rRNA, then enzymes guided by small RNAs retouch it and cut it up.
1371: One 13.3 kb pre-rRNA, more than 200 chemical retouches, three mature rRNAs (18S, 5.8S, 28S): nearly half of the transcript is discarded.
1373: Polymerase I adds a nucleotide to the pre-rRNA about 95 times per second: the same chemical move as the other polymerases.
